dedupe_keys.name: south africa living near waste sites and health national panel and geospatial analysis 2008 to 2015

description: This case study measures how exposure to waste sites relates to health across South Africa. The authors, researchers at the University of KwaZulu-Natal, the Africa Health Research Institute, the University of Cincinnati, the University of Exeter, University College London, the University of Lincoln and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, linked the nationally representative South African National Income Dynamics Study (SA-NIDS) panel, with health reports for 32,255 people, to waste site locations from the South Africa Waste Information System, and published the analysis in an open-access journal article. Exposure is the distance from each household to the nearest waste site. Coverage is national, 2008 to 2015. The article is free to read under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives licence. Caveats: the study is observational, distance is a proxy for exposure, and health outcomes are self-reported. The study found that the median distance from households to a waste site fell from 68.3 km to 8.5 km over the period, and that living within 5 km of a waste site was associated with asthma (relative risk 1.41), tuberculosis (1.18), diabetes (1.25) and depression (1.08) after controlling for socioeconomic factors. Simulation uses: exposure-response parameters for siting waste facilities and assessing the health burden of waste infrastructure. Related records: the Deonar landfill household health survey (data-deonar-landfill-household-health-survey) studies health near a landfill in India.
